WAL-CLM-DDDL-000008.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000008.question: How did Wallach first connect diabetes to a mineral deficiency?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000008.answer_short: From the autopsy table: he saw zoo marmosets, alligators and shrews die of diabetes caused by chromium and vanadium deficiency.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000021.subject: absorption
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000021.question: What helps or blocks iron absorption?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000021.answer_short: Vitamin C sharply increases iron absorption, while clays and phytates work the other way and decrease it — so what you eat alongside a mineral changes how much you actually take up.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000034.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000034.question: How does vanadium help with diabetes?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000034.answer_short: Vanadium mimics insulin — it makes the cell's insulin receptors more sensitive, helping the body handle glucose and carbohydrates.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000048.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000048.question: How does Wallach treat diabetes?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000048.answer_short: Start with chromium and vanadium at 250 mcg a day in the early stages — carefully, to avoid dropping blood sugar too fast ('insulin shock').

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000053.subject: absorption
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000053.question: Are some 'diseases' really just malabsorption?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000053.answer_short: Wallach reframes conditions like asthma as malabsorption diseases — the real problem isn't the lungs but a gut failing to absorb essential fatty acids, manganese, and magnesium.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000095.subject: salt
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000095.question: Why does Wallach say to salt your food?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000095.answer_short: Salt (NaCl) is the raw material for stomach acid; salt-restricted diets breed achlorhydria and failed absorption -- so his treatment starts with salting your food to taste.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000096.subject: dietary_oils
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000096.question: Why does Wallach say heated vegetable and cooking oils are dangerous?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000096.answer_short: Heating or hydrogenating polyunsaturated oils turns them into trans fats and free-radical damage; with low selenium that's 'the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer.'

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000097.subject: dietary_oils
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000097.question: What causes age spots (liver spots), and how does Wallach treat them?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000097.answer_short: Age spots are rancid fat (ceroid lipofuscin / trans fatty acids) from cell walls surfacing in the skin — a cancer and heart-disease red flag; he cuts all fried foods and vegetable oils.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000098.subject: dietary_oils
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000098.question: What does Wallach say causes fibromyalgia?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000098.answer_short: He calls fibromyalgia a multiple-deficiency disease driven by a high intake of fried foods and vegetable oils plus low selenium, vitamin E and sulfur amino acids.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000099.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000099.question: How does Wallach say to cook eggs, and how much red meat, for Alzheimer's?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000099.answer_short: Soft-scrambled (not fried) eggs every day and 72 oz of red meat each month, to replace cholesterol needed to rebuild myelin.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000100.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000100.question: Are fried eggs bad, according to Wallach?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000100.answer_short: Yes -- Wallach says fried eggs precipitate 93% of gallbladder attacks (with fried onions, fried potatoes and pork close behind).

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000101.subject: meat
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000101.question: How often does Wallach say to eat meat, eggs and poultry for blood sugar?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000101.answer_short: Three to six times a day (cutting sugar and refined carbs) to stabilize blood sugar early in diabetes therapy.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000102.subject: meat
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000102.question: Why does Wallach say eggs and red meat are critical for MS, and what foods should be avoided?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000102.answer_short: Myelin is almost pure cholesterol, so eggs and red meat are vital; avoid fried foods and margarine and use fish/flax oil.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000103.subject: cruciferous_vegetables
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000103.question: Should people with hypothyroidism avoid cabbage and other cruciferous vegetables?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000103.answer_short: Wallach's hypothyroidism protocol begins by eliminating all goitrogenic foods such as nitrates and cabbage, then adds thyroid support.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000104.subject: water
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000104.question: Should you drink distilled water or filtered water?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000104.answer_short: Drink filtered water, not distilled - distilled water is 'hungry' and leaches minerals from your bones over long-term use.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000105.subject: carbonated_beverages
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000105.question: Are carbonated soft drinks bad for you?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000105.answer_short: Yes - Wallach says all carbonated soft drinks are loaded with phosphates that cause osteoporosis over the long haul.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000106.subject: butter
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000106.question: Is there ever a reason to cut back on butter?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000106.answer_short: Yes — the one cautionary note. For cerebrovascular disease (where Wallach calls vitamin D angiotoxic and a driver of arterial calcification), he says hold total vitamin D under 400 IU/day, and flags butter — alongside animal fat, cholesterol, milk, cereals, supplements and sunshine — as a notable dietary vitamin D contributor that makes staying under the cap difficult.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000108.subject: butter
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000108.question: Did the long-lived, disease-free cultures Wallach admires eat butter?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000108.answer_short: Yes — emphatically. In Wallach's analysis of the Hunza, the people he holds up as relatively disease-free and living well past 100, butter is a staple, not an afterthought: they put it in their tea and used it as a cooking shortening, and it sits among their core fat sources alongside whole milk, ghee, apricot oil and animal fats. Wallach lists it among the 14 Hunza practices he credits for their longevity.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000109.subject: beef
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000109.question: How much red meat does Wallach recommend eating during menopause?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000109.answer_short: For menopause, Wallach's protocol includes eating red meat once each day, plus 2 eggs daily and a monthly liver flush, on top of the base-line supplements and calcium/magnesium.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000110.subject: beef
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000110.question: Why does Wallach tell some people to cut back on red meat?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000110.answer_short: Because red meat is heavy in phosphorus relative to calcium; for bone/phosphorus-driven conditions like Paget's disease he says to reduce or eliminate red meat to correct the calcium/phosphorus ratio, the same logic that recurs for periodontal disease, triglycerides and hypertension.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000111.subject: pork
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000111.question: Is fried pork bad for you according to Wallach?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000111.answer_short: Wallach credits the longer average lifespan of Mormons and Seventh-Day Adventists partly to their avoidance of fried foods, and he lists fried pork first among the fried foods to skip.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000112.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000112.question: Is egg a high-quality protein compared to other foods?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000112.answer_short: Whole egg tops Wallach's protein chart with a chemical score of 100 and 94% utilization, higher than human milk, cow's milk, or soybean, making it his benchmark for usable protein.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000114.subject: fish
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000114.question: Does fish contain germanium?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000114.answer_short: Yes, but only a trace — and it is not a reason to eat tuna. Germanium is a trace element Wallach prizes as an immune booster (it stimulates natural killer cells, interferon, macrophages and T-suppressor cells) and an oxygen-utilization cofactor, with deficiency typified by a severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy and cancer. But tuna carries only about 2.3 ppm of germanium — actually less than ordinary beans at 4.67 ppm, and far below the germanium-rich healing herbs and foods like garlic, ginseng and shiitake mushrooms (100 to 2,000 ppm). So fish is a minor incidental source at best — not a meaningful way to get germanium.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000116.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000116.question: Where did plant-derived colloidal minerals come from?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000116.answer_short: Wallach traces the whole category to Mineral Toddy — a liquid he found at Hospital Santa Monica, drawn from a prehistoric plant deposit that never became oil, coal, or stone.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000117.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000117.question: Why does he say plant-derived beats ground-up rock?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000117.answer_short: Two claims in one sentence: 77 minerals in the bottle (more than the 60 he counts as essential), and up to 98% absorbable — because plants made them, not a mill.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000118.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000118.question: Why do plants matter to your minerals?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000118.answer_short: The single step at the heart of his whole framework — plants pull rock minerals out of the soil and rebuild them inside their own cells into the form living cells can actually use. A step your body can't do for itself.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000119.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000119.question: What do the world's longest-lived peoples all share?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000119.answer_short: Not genes — what grows in their fields. Every "Age Beater" culture settled below a glacier and built canals to bring its mineral-rich meltwater ('glacial milk') to their crops, which converted those inorganic minerals into plant-derived colloidal form.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000120.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000120.question: What can these minerals NOT do on their own?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000120.answer_short: Wallach's own honest limit on Mineral Toddy: every mineral in it is present only in tiny amounts. To hit even mainstream RDAs for calcium, magnesium, manganese, zinc, and potassium, you need a separate major-mineral source alongside it.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000121.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000121.question: Where is Wallach's “Fountain of Youth”?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000121.answer_short: Under our feet the whole time — it's minerals. After millennia of chasing longevity, Wallach says the answer is almost anticlimactic: the plant-derived minerals in the ground.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000122.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000122.question: What does the liquid mineral supplement taste like?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000122.answer_short: Intensely astringent — Wallach says drunk straight it would “shrink wrap your lips over your teeth,” so it's taken stirred into juice.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000123.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000123.question: How did Wallach discover colloidal minerals?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000123.answer_short: He'd never heard of them until he met the liquid being served to patients at Hospital Santa Monica, then spent three months reading everything then known about colloids.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000124.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000124.question: Does the source of plant-derived minerals matter — and what if a maker cuts corners?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000124.answer_short: Yes — quality tracks the source deposit. Wallach tells how a product went black and green batch-to-batch after its bottler switched to a cheaper source, and how he fixed it by going back to the original deposit under his own label.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000125.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000125.question: Why does Wallach point to the long-lived cultures as proof?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000125.answer_short: He treats them as a living “control group” — five ancient peoples with disease-free longevity from steady access to all 90 essential nutrients, chiefly plant-derived colloidal minerals — and promises you can do the same.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000126.subject: microplastics
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000126.question: How do I detox microplastics and plastics from my body?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000126.answer_short: Wallach never wrote about microplastics, but they're a xenobiotic — a foreign chemical the body must clear — and he endorses selenium's role in the 'detoxification of metals and certain xenobiotics.'

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000127.subject: detox
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000127.question: What is Wallach's routine for detoxing and clearing toxic metals?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000127.answer_short: Take alfalfa daily as a detoxifier, do a monthly apple-juice liver flush, and get a yearly hair analysis to track your toxic-metal load.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000128.subject: digestion
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000128.question: Does everyone get low stomach acid as they age?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000128.answer_short: Largely yes — Wallach calls achlorhydria a natural process of aging and “perhaps the most significant aging phenomenon,” and puts the number at 75 percent of people over 50 needing supplemental stomach acid. He names stress as the other cause, and says it lowers acid rather than raising it.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000129.subject: digestion
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000129.question: Is indigestion actually serious?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000129.answer_short: Wallach calls dyspepsia probably the most common “disease” in the western world and the most costly — but says the money is the smaller cost, because chronic indigestion leads on to food allergies, osteoporosis, anemia, a debilitated immune system and degenerative disease.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000130.subject: digestion
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000130.question: Are antacids bad for you?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000130.answer_short: In an emergency, no — Wallach calls them a good temporary fix. As a habit, yes: regular use will eventually damage you by reducing the nutrients you absorb, because the underlying problem is usually too little stomach acid, not too much.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000131.subject: digestion
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000131.question: Should I be taking digestive enzymes?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000131.answer_short: Wallach’s rule of thumb: as you grow older, take betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal decline in stomach-acid production — and be sure to take them if you are under stress.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000132.subject: digestion
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000132.question: Why do I get bloated after eating?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000132.answer_short: Because the stomach isn’t acidic enough to stay sterile. Wallach says low stomach acid lets bacteria and yeast from the small intestine migrate up into the stomach, where they ferment the carbohydrates and sugars in your meal — and that fermentation is the gas.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000133.subject: digestion
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000133.question: Why do pancreatic enzymes stop working?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000133.answer_short: They need an alkaline environment. Wallach explains it through dumping syndrome — when the stomach empties into the small intestine all at once it overloads the intestine’s natural buffer, and the acid conditions that result stop pancreatic enzymes from working properly.

WAL-CLM-DDDL-000134.subject: digestion
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000134.question: What is the pH of stomach acid?
WAL-CLM-DDDL-000134.answer_short: About 1.0. Wallach gives the body’s secretions as running from 1.0 in stomach acid up to 8.2 in pancreatic juice — a deliberately wide spread, in contrast to blood, which is held in the narrow band of 7.36 to 7.44.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000008.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000008.question: What does Wallach say happens in the brain to cause homosexuality?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000008.answer_short: Wallach groups homosexuality with intersex conditions as congenital, not a choice -- but the preoptic-hypothalamus mechanism (brain's sense of gender diverging from the genetic gender in the chromosomes) he states about intersex gender-assignment, calling physically-normal gay individuals 'less understood' and distinct.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000009.subject: intersex
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000009.question: What causes intersex conditions, and can they be prevented?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000009.answer_short: Wallach ties them to mineral or vitamin deficiency in the embryo -- citing John Money's estimate of up to 4% of births -- and argues they could be avoided with complete preconception nutrition.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000017.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000017.question: How were birth defects explained before modern medicine?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000017.answer_short: Wallach surveys centuries of theories -- Renaissance omens and divine punishment, early teratology collections -- up to the 1961 thalidomide disaster that proved drugs can deform a fetus.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000018.subject: pregnancy_birth
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000018.question: What does Wallach say is the most common cause of birth defects?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000018.answer_short: Deficiency of one or more of the 90 essential nutrients in the mother before conception and through the first 90 days of pregnancy -- proven, he says, by an animal industry that breeds out birth defects with nutrition.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000019.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000019.question: Does Wallach think homosexuality is a lifestyle choice?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000019.answer_short: No. Wallach reframes it as a prenatal, congenital event -- a preventable deficiency of minerals or vitamins in early pregnancy, not a learned behavior or a choice.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000020.subject: intersex
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000020.question: What does 'intersex' mean?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000020.answer_short: Intersex is the modern medical term for what was once called hermaphroditism -- a range of congenital variations in sexual anatomy; one 1969 catalogue listed 98 distinct types.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000021.subject: intersex
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000021.question: How have intersex and homosexual people been regarded through history?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000021.answer_short: Wallach traces it from Plato's 'three sexes' and the Hermes-plus-Aphrodite root of 'hermaphrodite' through executions of intersex people to modern cases like Christine Jorgenson and Olympic sex testing.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000022.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000022.question: What brain-anatomy research does Wallach cite on homosexuality?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000022.answer_short: He cites Simon LeVay's autopsy studies finding the preoptic hypothalamus smaller in homosexual men, plus differences in the anterior commissure and a prenatal testosterone surge.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000023.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000023.question: Is there a 'gay gene'?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000023.answer_short: Wallach says no -- identical twins are only about 50% concordant, so he argues it is congenital but not genetic; he quotes geneticist Dean Hamer that there is no gay gene.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000024.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000024.question: Why does Wallach think homosexuality has become more common?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000024.answer_short: He ties the rise in reported homosexuality to the steady decline of minerals in farm soils and the food supply, citing Kinsey and later prevalence figures.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000025.subject: intersex
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000025.question: What do animals reveal about intersex birth defects?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000025.answer_short: Every human congenital sexual defect also appears in animals from embryonic malnutrition -- like the 'freemartin,' a masculinized female calf twinned with a male; scarcer nutrition means more defects.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000026.subject: homosexuality
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000026.question: Does Wallach think homosexuality can be prevented?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000026.answer_short: He says a complete preconception nutrition program -- the 90 essential nutrients -- could prevent it; from his interviews he holds it is congenital, so it cannot be prayed away or coached away.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000027.subject: quackbusters
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000027.question: What are the 'Quackbusters' and what does Wallach say about them?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000027.answer_short: Wallach calls the Quackbusters a group of doctors organized to destroy alternative-medicine competition, and rejects their claim that a varied diet alone supplies all the vitamins and minerals you need.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000028.subject: longevity
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000028.question: What did a Harvard survey find about where Americans live longest?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000028.answer_short: A 1990 survey found the longest-living Americans were Scandinavian-heritage dairy farmers who poached, stewed and baked their food, while the shortest-lived regions fried everything -- diet, not doctors, drove the gap.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000029.subject: absorption
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000029.question: How does low stomach acid block absorption?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000029.answer_short: Stomach acid — made from ordinary salt — is required to absorb vitamin B12, activate the protein enzyme pepsin, and take up minerals. When acid runs low (hypochlorhydria), absorption fails.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000030.subject: gluten
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000030.question: Why is gluten so damaging to the gut?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000030.answer_short: Wallach frames gluten not as an allergy but a 'contact enteritis' — like poison ivy, but on the gut lining — that gradually destroys the intestinal villi and leaves you unable to absorb nutrients.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000060.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000060.question: Why are the minerals in ordinary supplement tablets so poorly absorbed?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000060.answer_short: Because of their form. Wallach says metallic minerals (the gluconate/carbonate/oxide forms in most tablets, plus eggshell, oyster shell, dolomite and antacids) are only 8–12% absorbable — and just 3–5% after age 35–40. Chelated minerals absorb better, but plant-derived colloidal minerals are the most usable, which is why he calls them the most critical of the 90 essential nutrients.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000140.subject: absorption
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000140.question: Is it what you eat, or what you absorb?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000140.answer_short: Wallach flips the old adage: your health isn't decided by what you eat but by what you actually absorb — the cornerstone of his two-pronged model (supply the 90, and fix the gut so they get in).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000141.subject: gluten
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000141.question: How common is gluten intolerance?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000141.answer_short: About a third of Americans — 115 million people — are gluten intolerant per a 2009 Mayo Clinic study Wallach cites, and far more in high-grain communities.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000142.subject: gluten
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000142.question: If gluten damaged my gut, what's the fix?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000142.answer_short: Two prongs together: go fully gluten-free AND supply the 90 essential nutrients (plus therapeutic doses of what you're most short on). Wallach says the combination resolves many chronic problems.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000143.subject: phytates
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000143.question: Why does Wallach say phytates in nuts, grains, and seeds block calcium?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000143.answer_short: Phytic acid in nuts, grain bran, seeds, oatmeal and whole wheat binds calcium into insoluble calcium phytate the body can't absorb.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000144.subject: phytates
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000144.question: Which foods does Wallach say block calcium with oxalic acid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000144.answer_short: Oxalic acid in rhubarb, spinach, chard and greens binds calcium into insoluble calcium oxalate that isn't absorbed; fiber blocks it too.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000145.subject: phytates
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000145.question: Does Wallach say to soak or sprout nuts, grains, and seeds?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000145.answer_short: In healthy traditional diets, Wallach notes seeds, grains, and nuts are soaked, sprouted, and fermented before eating.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000146.subject: sugar
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000146.question: Does caffeine leach calcium from your bones?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000146.answer_short: Too much caffeine pulls calcium out of the body's bone reserves.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000147.subject: carbonated_beverages
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000147.question: Why does Wallach say soft drinks throw off your calcium-phosphorus balance?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000147.answer_short: Diet calcium-to-phosphorus should be 2:1; soft drinks are high-phosphorus junk food that wrecks the balance.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000148.subject: dietary_oils
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000148.question: How does Wallach connect fried foods and oxidized oils to brain and nerve diseases?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000148.answer_short: He blames free-radical brain damage on regular gluten, fried foods, burnt animal fat, oxidized dietary oils, nitrate-processed meats, and excess mono/polyunsaturated oils.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000149.subject: dietary_oils
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000149.question: What does Wallach say overusing dietary oils and eating fried foods does to the body?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000149.answer_short: He calls it self-destruction: too many fried/burnt foods and overused margarines, salad dressings and cooking oils load the body with trans fats, heterocyclic amines and acrylamides.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000150.subject: dietary_oils
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000150.question: Why does Wallach say vegetable oils like corn oil worsen selenium deficiency?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000150.answer_short: Corn oil is 'notorious for increasing the need for selenium' — extra dietary oil creates a relative selenium deficiency even when selenium is otherwise present in the diet.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000151.subject: cholesterol
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000151.question: Does Wallach consider cholesterol essential, and what happens if you're deficient?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000151.answer_short: Wallach treats cholesterol as vital, and argues its deficiency produces specific disease states — among them Alzheimer's disease, type 2 diabetes, erectile dysfunction, low testosterone, menopause symptoms and adrenal exhaustion.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000153.subject: cholesterol
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000153.question: How much fat did healthy traditional diets contain, according to Wallach?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000153.answer_short: Per Weston Price, traditional diets were 30-80% fat, but only about 4% of calories came from polyunsaturated oils — the rest was saturated and monounsaturated fat.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000154.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000154.question: How many eggs a day does Wallach recommend, and how should they be cooked?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000154.answer_short: Four to six eggs per day per 100 lb of body weight -- poached, soft-boiled, or scrambled in butter (never fried).

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000155.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000155.question: Why did Wallach tell a Parkinson's patient to eat a dozen-plus poached eggs a day?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000155.answer_short: To rebuild myelin -- 12 to 14 poached eggs daily supply the raw materials, while avoiding trans fats, heterocyclic amines and acrylamides.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000156.subject: dairy
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000156.question: What does Wallach think of pasteurized milk and low-fat foods?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000156.answer_short: He counts pasteurized milk and low-fat foods among the harmful 'displacing foods of modern commerce', favoring full-fat whole foods.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000157.subject: processed_meat
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000157.question: Which processed meats does Wallach say to avoid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000157.answer_short: Deli slices, sandwich meats, sausage, bologna, salami, pepperoni, jerky, hamburger patties, meatloaf, meatballs and canned meats.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000158.subject: gluten
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000158.question: Which grains contain the gluten Wallach says to avoid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000158.answer_short: Wheat, barley, rye, and oats -- the 'small-grain' proteins. Wallach calls the reaction an intolerance (a 'contact enteritis'), not a true allergy.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000159.subject: gluten
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000159.question: How long has gluten intolerance been recognized?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000159.answer_short: It is not new: Wallach says Egyptian and Greek physicians recognized this bad reaction to grain thousands of years ago.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000160.subject: cruciferous_vegetables
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000160.question: Are cruciferous vegetables like broccoli and kale bad for the thyroid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000160.answer_short: Wallach lists cruciferous vegetables — cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kale — as goitrogens that interfere with normal thyroid metabolism.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000161.subject: water
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000161.question: Is alkaline water good, and when should you drink it?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000161.answer_short: Drink clean, slightly alkaline water (7.5-8.5) - but not with meals, since it neutralizes the stomach acid you need to digest.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000162.subject: butter
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000162.question: What vitamins does butter give you, and why do they matter?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000162.answer_short: Citing Weston Price, Wallach names butter as a leading source of fat-soluble vitamins A and D — traditional diets delivered about 10 times these versus the modern American diet. Those fat-soluble vitamins are the catalysts required for efficient mineral absorption; without them you cannot absorb minerals no matter how abundant. Butter is therefore an absorption-enabler, not a food to shun.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000163.subject: butter
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000163.question: Is grass-fed butter different, and what special nutrient does it contain?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000163.answer_short: Wallach (via Price) says butter carries "Activator X" — now thought to be vitamin K2 — but specifically butter made from the milk of cows grazing rapidly-growing green spring and fall grass. It is a pointed endorsement of real, grass-fed, seasonal butter as a source of a hard-to-get fat-soluble nutrient.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000164.subject: butter
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000164.question: Can a lack of butter actually cause disease?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000164.answer_short: Wallach recounts the discovery of vitamin A: lab animals on lard-only fat developed deficiency with xerophthalmia (dry, diseased eyes) that was corrected by adding butter, egg yolk and cod liver oil. In humans, WWI-era xerophthalmia was traced directly to reduced access to dietary butter — losing butter caused the eye disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000165.subject: butter
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000165.question: Has butter been used to treat a disease?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000165.answer_short: Wallach recounts that the French physician Armand Trousseau treated rickets patients with cod liver oil, sunshine, AND butter — an early demonstration that diet plus sunshine (vitamin D) cause, prevent and cure rickets. Butter appears as part of a real historical therapeutic regimen.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000166.subject: beef
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000166.question: Can you catch mad cow disease from eating beef, according to Wallach?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000166.answer_short: Wallach says no. He argues BSE ('mad cow') and CJD are actually copper-deficiency diseases, not infections, because every attempt to transmit them by injecting infected brain tissue failed to satisfy Koch's postulates.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000167.subject: beef
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000167.question: What is beef liver good for, and is there a history behind it?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000167.answer_short: Beef liver is a rich vitamin A source; Wallach notes the ancient Egyptians cured night blindness around 1,000 BC with beef-liver-juice extracts, which worked because vitamin A, stored in the liver, fixes the deficiency.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000168.subject: pork
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000168.question: Is pork good for building muscle or for muscular dystrophy?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000168.answer_short: Wallach does name pork chops as the first of the 'muscle meats' — the meats where, as he puts it, muscle meat is 'King' — alongside beef steak, lamb chops, roasts, ground red meat, chicken and turkey. But his actual point about muscular dystrophy (what veterinarians call white muscle disease) is that it has nothing to do with eating too little meat: he frames MD as a simple selenium-deficiency disease that is fully preventable and curable with extra selenium, a full 90-essential-nutrient program, and a gluten-free diet — the same selenium supplementation that 'wiped out' the disease in farm animals. He even warns that a gluten-damaged gut can't absorb selenium even when it's in the food ('you are not what you eat, you are what you absorb'). So pork is a fine muscle-meat protein, but eating pork is not his prescription for building muscle or beating MD — supplementing selenium is.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000169.subject: pork
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000169.question: What kinds of pork or meat products does Wallach tell people to avoid?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000169.answer_short: As a standing rule Wallach says to avoid processed meats such as sausage, deli slices, bologna, salami and pepperoni because of their nitrates, nitrites, and gluten-laden fillers.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000170.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000170.question: Are egg yolks a good source of vitamin D, and is avoiding them harmful?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000170.answer_short: Yes. Wallach calls egg yolks a good dietary source of vitamin D, and he treats the fear of their cholesterol as actively harmful. He blames 3 things for bringing rickets back in the industrialized world — heavy sunscreen use, the cholesterol-scare that made parents avoid egg yolks, and pediatricians telling parents to skip children's vitamin and mineral supplements — and points to a reported 400 percent rise in childhood rickets between 1995 and 2011 as the result. He labels the resurgence a 'physician-caused disease.'

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000171.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000171.question: What nutrient do eggs supply that Wallach ties to disease prevention?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000171.answer_short: Selenium. Wallach names eggs as one of the everyday food sources of selenium — alongside liver, kidneys, and some high-selenium rice — and he calls this trace element the key to both preventing and curing cystic fibrosis. In his telling CF is not a genetic disease at all but a selenium deficiency during the first 3 months of pregnancy. He notes it strikes about 1 in every 2,500 American children, is usually fatal in infancy with fewer than half of victims living past age 21, yet insists it is essentially 100 percent curable when caught within 30 days of birth — which is why he treats selenium-bearing foods like eggs as genuinely protective.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000172.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000172.question: How many eggs does Wallach recommend for multiple sclerosis?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000172.answer_short: For multiple sclerosis, Wallach prescribes 6-8 eggs per day to supply the raw materials that maintain and repair the brain's myelin, paired with all 90 essential nutrients and antioxidants including selenium.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000173.subject: fish
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000173.question: Is it safe to eat a lot of fish — what about mercury?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000173.answer_short: Wallach's answer is nuanced, not a blanket 'avoid fish.' The mercury in fish is methyl mercury, and it bioaccumulates the more fish you eat — the real offenders being the large predator fish: shark, tuna, and swordfish. He lays the body-burden out in plain tiers: people who rarely eat fish carry very little mercury (about 2-5 ug/kg), moderate eaters sit 10 ug/kg, and heavy eaters of those big predators can climb to 400 ug/kg — on the order of 100 times the occasional eater. So the caution is aimed at loading up on the large predators, not at fish generally. Wallach also points to the protection built into his own framework: selenium and mercury are mutual antagonists, so keeping selenium adequate defends the body against the mercury it does take in.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000174.subject: fish
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000174.question: Where did cod liver oil's reputation as a cure come from?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000174.answer_short: Scottish fishermen used cod-liver oil to prevent and cure rickets long before doctors accepted it; the French physician Trousseau confirmed it with cod-liver oil, sunshine, and butter — while orthodox medicine kept hunting for a 'rickets germ.'

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000175.subject: fish
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000175.question: What foods are high in vitamin A — is fish one?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000175.answer_short: Yes — fish liver is one of the richest sources of preformed vitamin A, the ready-to-use form called retinol, with cod-liver oil the classic example. Wallach draws the useful line here: this animal-derived retinol is already active, unlike the carotene (provitamin A) your body has to convert out of brightly pigmented plants. The same early vitamin-A research pointed to butter and egg yolk alongside cod-liver oil as the animal foods that reversed the deficiency — so fish sits with butter and eggs among the top preformed-A foods.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000176.subject: fish
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000176.question: Do fish contain vitamin K / the fat-soluble 'Activator X'?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000176.answer_short: Yes, and it matters more than it first sounds. Fish livers and shellfish are one of the few sources of the fat-soluble factor Weston Price named 'Activator X' — now believed to be vitamin K2 — which every healthy traditional culture had in its diet. Its importance is all about absorption: Price found that the fat-soluble vitamins A, D and Activator X act as the catalysts that let the body actually take up minerals and use protein, and that without them a person cannot absorb minerals no matter how abundant they are in the food. Those primitive diets supplied roughly 10 times the fat-soluble vitamins of the modern American diet — which is a large part of why they were so free of degenerative disease.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000177.subject: fish
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000177.question: Can fish oil ever be harmful?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000177.answer_short: Wallach warns that a high intake of polyunsaturated oils including fish oil, if you're selenium-deficient, raises the risk of birth defects, arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, sudden heart death, and cancer — because the unprotected oils go rancid in your cells.

WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000178.subject: antioxidants
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000178.question: Do flavonoids raise your ORAC?
WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000178.answer_short: Yes - Wallach lists raising ORAC antioxidant activity among the effects demonstrated clinically in people, not just in cell studies.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000001.subject: beef
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000001.question: Does Dr. Wallach think beef and red meat are good for you?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000001.answer_short: Wallach calls red meat an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids, and says the only trick is to cook it no more than medium, since well-done or burnt fat forms heterocyclic amines. He even recommends raw steak tartare.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000002.subject: beef
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000002.question: Is it dangerous to eat beef cooked well done?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000002.answer_short: Wallach cites a study of 930 women where eating beef and pork very well done raised breast-cancer risk 462% versus medium-rare; his point is that it is not the fat that harms you but how you cook it, because burnt animal fat becomes heterocyclic amines, powerful carcinogens.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000003.subject: beef
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000003.question: How does fattening beef cattle explain human obesity in Wallach's view?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000003.answer_short: Wallach's 'Feedlot Syndrome' analogy: ranchers fatten beef cattle on a steady stream of carbohydrate feed paired with optimal nutrients that drive the animal to eat with endless, fervent hunger, growing a 40-lb calf to 900-1,100 lb in a year. He argues humans are fattened by the same carb-heavy diet — but, unlike the optimally-supplemented cattle, humans eat it while mineral-deficient, which is what leaves them with a ravenous appetite.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000004.subject: pork
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000004.question: Does eating a lot of pork cause obesity and diabetes?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000004.answer_short: Not on its own, in Wallach's view. He points to the Old Order Amish, who eat pork, beef, goat and mutton 3 times a day plus heavy whole milk, butter and cheese — by his account consuming more sugar, fat, red meat and dairy than anyone in North America — and yet post an obesity rate of just 4% and a type-II diabetes rate of just 6%, only about a tenth and a half, respectively, of their 'modern' neighbors in the very same county. He credits that gap not to their meat-heavy diet, and not even to their hard farm labor (the horses do most of the work), but to the essential minerals in the wood ashes they spread on their garden soil every single morning.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000005.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000005.question: Are eggs actually bad for you, like doctors say?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000005.answer_short: Wallach cites a Scientific American longevity summary: the patients who followed doctors' advice to the letter didn't reach 100, while the 'rebellious' ones who ate salt, eggs, red meat, butter and chicken skin did.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000006.subject: eggs
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000006.question: How did eggs help cure pellagra historically?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000006.answer_short: Pellagra turned out to be a dietary deficiency disease — a lack of vitamin B3 (niacin) — and eggs were part of the fix. Wallach recounts how a U.S. Public Health Service researcher noticed that in orphanages and mental asylums the residents came down with pellagra while the staff, who ate a wider variety of food, stayed well. When eggs and milk were simply added to the sufferers' diets, the pellagra disappeared. Wallach lays out the competing theories of the era — the main one blamed the limited corn diet, while some held that pellagra was an insect-borne disease like malaria or yellow fever — and this is his illustration that nutrient-dense foods like eggs can reverse a 'disease' that was really malnutrition.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000008.subject: fish
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000008.question: Did Wallach have a hand in the official omega-3 / heart-health claim?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000008.answer_short: Yes — and it was more than a footnote. Wallach was a co-petitioner on the FDA petition (Docket No. 03Q-0401, filed 6/23/2003) that won the qualified health claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk, which the FDA allowed on 9/8/2004. It matters because it was one front in Wallach's larger legal war against the FDA — waged with First Amendment attorney Jonathan Emord — to force the agency to let supplement makers state health benefits that were actually proven. The same campaign carried his solo selenium-and-cancer claim (approved 4/28/2003); as he tells it, after losing every battle before the 1994 DSHEA Act, his side won every one that followed. So the official omega-3 heart-health language products can now use is partly his doing.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000009.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000009.question: How much of the liquid mineral supplement should I take?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000009.answer_short: One ounce of plant-derived colloidal minerals per 100 lb of body weight a day, ideally split — a 100-lb person takes 1 oz (½ oz twice daily), a 200-lb person 2 oz. Raise to 1¼ oz per 100 lb to lose 25+ lb.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000010.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000010.question: What can I do about sugar cravings and the munchies?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000010.answer_short: Take one ounce of plant-derived colloidal minerals per 100 lb of body weight — even up to 10× a day early on. Wallach reads cravings and pica as a sure sign of mineral deficiency.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000011.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000011.question: How do I re-mineralize distilled or filtered water?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000011.answer_short: Add one ounce of liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals to each gallon of distilled or double-filtered water — distilled is mineral-free and otherwise leaches minerals from the body.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000012.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000012.question: Is there a study showing the minerals help with diabetes or obesity?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000012.answer_short: Wallach cites a 2004 pilot study he co-authored among the Nez Perce of Idaho: on a plant-derived colloidal mineral program, participants lost weight, lowered blood pressure, and cut fasting blood sugar 30–50%, most reducing or stopping medication.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000013.subject: orac
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000013.question: What does ORAC stand for?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000013.answer_short: Oxygen Radical Absorbance Capacity - a lab score for how strongly a food, drink or supplement neutralizes free radicals.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000014.subject: antioxidants
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000014.question: What are the top ten antioxidant foods?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000014.answer_short: Prunes lead at 5,770 per 100 g, then raisins, blueberries, blackberries and kale.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000015.subject: orac
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000015.question: How do I actually get more ORAC into my day?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000015.answer_short: Swap your salad dressing for a high-ORAC juice - noni or mangosteen - instead of oil.

WAL-CLM-HELLS-000016.subject: antioxidants
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000016.question: Why do I need more antioxidants when I'm losing weight?
WAL-CLM-HELLS-000016.answer_short: Because burning fat generates free radicals - losing weight itself creates the damage antioxidants defend against.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000018.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000018.question: Why do the 90 essential nutrients matter?
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000018.answer_short: They're the cofactors enzymes need to work - miss one and the enzyme stalls. Most people never reach optimal levels, a 'subclinical' shortfall felt as fatigue and low mood.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000019.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000019.question: Can you get all your nutrition from food alone?
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000019.answer_short: Wallach says no - food itself is depleted (vitamins down 37%, trace minerals 77%), so he calls a full 90-nutrient supplement program a cornerstone of health.

WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000020.subject: wallach
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000020.question: What are Dr. Wallach's credentials?
WAL-CLM-IAIYH-000020.answer_short: A 1991 Nobel Prize nomination for linking selenium to cystic fibrosis, two research medals, co-author of the DSHEA supplement law, and credit as an early founder of epigenetics.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000002.subject: wallach
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000002.question: What makes Dr. Wallach's approach different?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000002.answer_short: 20,000+ autopsies across 454 animal species plus 3,000 humans — a comparative-pathology record that led him to conclude 'natural causes' deaths were really nutritional deficiencies.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000003.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000003.question: Are carbohydrates an essential nutrient?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000003.answer_short: No, says Wallach - the body can make all the carbs and sugar it needs by breaking down and rebuilding fats and proteins, so none has to come from the diet.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000004.subject: amino_acids
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000004.question: How many essential amino acids are there?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000004.answer_short: Wallach counts 12 the body can't make. Miss any for long and a specific deficiency disease follows.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000005.subject: wallach
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000005.question: How did Wallach beat the FDA over omega-3?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000005.answer_short: After a long legal fight, on Sept 8, 2004 the FDA let his petition stand — allowing the claim that omega-3s cut heart-disease risk, which had been illegal to state for 65 years.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000006.subject: cholesterol
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000006.question: Is cholesterol bad for you?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000006.answer_short: No — Wallach calls cholesterol an essential nutrient: it builds every cell membrane, all the steroid hormones, and the brain's myelin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000007.subject: vitamins
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000007.question: What happens if you're vitamin-deficient during pregnancy?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000007.answer_short: Wallach warns it can cause catastrophic birth defects - among them neural-tube defects, cleft lip and palate, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis and heart defects.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000009.subject: vitamins
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000009.question: Does the birth-control pill deplete a vitamin?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000009.answer_short: Yes - Wallach says 15-20% of women on the pill show vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency: malaise, depression, and glucose intolerance (trouble handling blood sugar).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000010.subject: wallach
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000010.question: Does Wallach agree with Linus Pauling?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000010.answer_short: Not on minerals — he corrects even the two-time Nobel laureate, who dismissed minerals as secondary and capped selenium at 15 mcg (today's safe limit is 200–1,000 mcg).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000013.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000013.question: How depleted is the food supply?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000013.answer_short: A USDA comparison (1975-2004) shows steep losses - broccoli lost 54% of its calcium, apples 60% of their iron - so Wallach says food alone can't supply enough minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000014.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000014.question: What are the 90 essential nutrients?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000014.answer_short: Of 79+ elements found in the body, Wallach counts 60 minerals as essential - plus 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids and 3 essential fatty acids: the '90 essentials.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000017.subject: essential_nutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000017.question: How does a mineral deficiency progress before you notice?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000017.answer_short: In four hidden stages: initial (just 'low energy,' tests normal), compensated (cravings, odd symptoms), decompensated (real disease), then clinical (full disease, even death).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000023.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000023.question: What are chelated minerals, and do they absorb better?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000023.answer_short: Chelated minerals wrap an amino acid around each mineral, absorbing ~40–65% — a 400% jump over metallic (8–12%); on a label they read as 'picolinate' or 'amino acid chelate.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000024.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000024.question: What actually is a 'colloidal' mineral?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000024.answer_short: An ultra-fine particle. Wallach describes a colloidal mineral as a particle so small (~1 billion would fit in 0.01 cubic inch) it can't be seen with the naked eye, and which stays grouped together instead of separating into individual atoms the way salt does in water — kept within the 1–100 nanometer range he calls 'nano-technology.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000025.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000025.question: Why can't you just swallow ground-up rock minerals?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000025.answer_short: Inorganic mineral particles are too large to cross the gut wall; only when amino acids convert them into absorbable 'crystalloids' can the intestine take them up.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000026.subject: colloidal_minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000026.question: Which form of colloidal mineral is best?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000026.answer_short: The plant-derived, living organic colloid — coated in a water-loving protein, up to 98% bioavailable — is the form Wallach favors over bare 'rock flour' or industrial versions.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000031.subject: silver
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000031.question: What was colloidal silver used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000031.answer_short: Wallach relays older medical reports (not his own protocol): in 1917-18 colloidal silver was described as soothing inflammation and helping prostate/bladder irritation, itching, catarrh, even a post-childbirth blood infection. Silver sulfadiazine is still used in ~70% of U.S. burn centers.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000033.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000033.question: Is aluminum in our food, and is that dangerous?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000033.answer_short: Unavoidable but normal, Wallach says: aluminum is Earth's most abundant metal (~12% of crust) and every plant takes it up - so no food or natural water is free of it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000034.subject: aluminum
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000034.question: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000034.answer_short: Wallach says no - he calls it a myth from 'a single faulty study,' citing later work (Oxford 1992, a 2007 German assessment) that found no proven dietary-aluminum link.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000035.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000035.question: What is actinium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000035.answer_short: A naturally radioactive metal that glows in the dark like radium (its name is Greek for 'ray'). Wallach lists it among elements found in living tissue -- it gathers in bone and liver, where he speculates it may have a metabolic role, though he assigns it no health use.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000040.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000040.question: Does gold treat arthritis?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000040.answer_short: Wallach is cautious - doctors add gold to aspirin for arthritis, but he stresses it only helps ACTIVE joint inflammation, not advanced, destructive rheumatoid arthritis.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000041.subject: gold
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000041.question: Is gold used to treat cancer?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000041.answer_short: One form is: gold-198, a short-lived radioactive isotope (2.7-day half-life), is used as radiation therapy for some cancers - a medical use Wallach notes, not nutrition.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000046.subject: bismuth
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000046.question: What is bismuth used for, and did stress really cause ulcers?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000046.answer_short: Bismuth is the pink in Pepto-Bismol, used for stomach ulcers and gut infections for millennia. Wallach's myth-buster: ulcers were blamed on stress historically, but the real cause is Helicobacter pylori bacteria (Marshall & Warren, 1983) -- treated with antibiotics, antacids and bismuth.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000048.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000048.question: Where does the word 'bromide' come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000048.answer_short: From medicine: sodium bromide, a bromine salt, was a common mild sedative in the late 1800s used to calm the nerves -- which is why we still speak of taking a 'bromide' to settle down.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000050.subject: carbon
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000050.question: What is Wallach's view on global warming?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000050.answer_short: Off nutrition, he is skeptical of blaming humans -- calling our share of Earth's biomass 'pitifully small' and noting Ice Ages and warm spells have always cycled naturally. His fix is simply to plant more trees, which pull carbon dioxide from the air. (His personal stance on a debated topic.)

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000051.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000051.question: What are carbohydrates?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000051.answer_short: The body's convenient fuel (but not essential) - plants build them from CO2 and water by photosynthesis. Sized as single sugars, double sugars, and long chains like starch and fiber.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000052.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000052.question: What are fats?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000052.answer_short: Water-repelling molecules packing ~9 calories a gram (vs 4.5); mostly triglycerides (glycerol + fatty acids). Fatty acids differ by chain length, saturation, and 'omega' number.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000054.subject: cholesterol
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000054.question: What does cholesterol actually do in the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000054.answer_short: It's the raw material for vitamin D, bile acids, and the adrenal stress and sex hormones — so a cholesterol deficiency can worsen menopause and flatten libido.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000055.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000055.question: What are proteins?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000055.answer_short: The body's most abundant carbon compound - the main stuff of muscle and every cell, and enzymes are proteins too. Built from amino acids linked by peptide bonds; they add nitrogen.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000056.subject: macronutrients
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000056.question: Can you eat too much protein?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000056.answer_short: Wallach's view: a healthy person can eat even 300 g of protein a day (nearly 3/4 lb of meat) with no harm - as long as they have no kidney or liver disease and supplement properly.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000057.subject: amino_acids
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000057.question: What does each amino acid do?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000057.answer_short: Many build protein (valine, lysine, leucine...); tryptophan makes niacin and serotonin; phenylalanine makes thyroid hormone and adrenaline; methionine makes choline and creatine.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000059.subject: vitamins
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000059.question: What are vitamins?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000059.answer_short: Organic compounds the body needs in tiny daily amounts but can't make itself; they work mostly as coenzymes (switching enzymes on) and supply no calories and no body mass.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000062.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000062.question: How much calcium are humans designed to eat?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000062.answer_short: Wallach argues we're built for Stone-Age intakes of 1,600–3,000 mg a day; modern Americans get a fraction — as little as 300 mg.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000065.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000065.question: How much calcium is in your body, and where?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000065.answer_short: Calcium is the body's most abundant mineral (~1–1.2 kg); 99% sits in the bones and teeth, and the last 1% works in blood and cells.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000066.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000066.question: How is calcium stored in your bones?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000066.answer_short: As hydroxyapatite crystals on a protein 'bone matrix' — soak a bone in vinegar two weeks and the calcium leaches out, leaving the bendy scaffold.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000067.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000067.question: What does calcium do besides build bone?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000067.answer_short: It's a working cofactor: it releases ATP energy for muscle, drives blood clotting, moves signals across membranes, fires nerves and paces the heartbeat.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000068.subject: absorption
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000068.question: What blocks calcium from being absorbed?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000068.answer_short: It depends on the form and the gut: a metallic calcium pill may be only 1–3% absorbed, and phytates in grains, low stomach acid, celiac damage, sugar and carbonation all drive it lower.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000069.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000069.question: How does the body keep blood calcium steady?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000069.answer_short: Two hormones — parathormone and calcitonin — hold serum calcium at 8.5–10.5 mg/dL, mostly by borrowing it from and returning it to bone.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000070.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000070.question: What in the modern diet drains your calcium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000070.answer_short: Fiber, salt and soft-drink phosphate force calcium out of the body — the modern diet's calcium-to-phosphorus ratio simply can't be met by eating alone.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000074.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000074.question: How many diseases does Wallach tie to calcium deficiency?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000074.answer_short: 147 — Wallach links no fewer than 147 diseases to calcium deficiency or imbalance, and says U.S. diets are so deficient that only supplements fix it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000075.subject: calcium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000075.question: Which famous people did Wallach say had calcium deficiency?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000075.answer_short: He points to Pope John Paul II, Elizabeth Taylor, 'Bo' Jackson and vegan NBA star Bill Walton — all, he says, with osteoporosis or fractures.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000078.subject: digestion
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000078.question: What does stomach acid actually do?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000078.answer_short: Salt (sodium chloride) is the raw material your stomach uses to make hydrochloric acid — and that acid is what activates pepsin to digest protein, activates intrinsic factor to absorb B12, and lets you absorb minerals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000081.subject: cobalt
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000081.question: Why can’t I absorb vitamin B12?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000081.answer_short: Because B12 uptake depends on stomach acid. Wallach explains that intrinsic factor only works when the stomach is acid enough; with hypochlorhydria it fails and B12 is not absorbed — which is why doctors give B12 shots to older people on salt-restricted diets.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000085.subject: cobalt
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000085.question: What does cobalt have to do with vitamin B12?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000085.answer_short: Cobalt is the heart of vitamin B12 -- it sits in a ring related to the ones holding iron in hemoglobin and magnesium in chlorophyll, and gives B12 its red color. 'Cyanocobalamine' was named for a cyanide group on the first B12 isolated (1948).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000086.subject: cobalt
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000086.question: How do animals get vitamin B12 from cobalt?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000086.answer_short: Microbes do the work: gut bacteria in a cow's rumen turn elemental cobalt into B12, which the animal absorbs. Carnivores get it secondhand from prey, and rabbits and rodents eat their own night feces (coprophagy) to recover it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000089.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000089.question: How does chromium deficiency lead to diabetes?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000089.answer_short: Chromium runs the body's blood-sugar handling; deficiency wrecks glucose tolerance (77% of 'normal' over-70s) — and Wallach cites the USDA that 90% of Americans are chromium-deficient.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000091.subject: chromium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000091.question: Why is chromium so easy to lose and hard to absorb?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000091.answer_short: Sugar flushes chromium out in urine (up 300% for 12 hrs) and food chromium is barely retained; form decides - ~25% of chelated vs up to 98% of colloidal is absorbed.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000092.subject: chromium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000092.question: Has Americans' chromium level been falling?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000092.answer_short: Yes - the young hold more chromium than the old, unsupplemented tissue steadily drops with age, and Wallach charts a steep fall in average American blood chromium since 1948.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000093.subject: chromium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000093.question: How was chromium discovered, and why does it color gemstones?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000093.answer_short: Found in 1797 by Vauquelin and named from Greek 'chroma' (color) for its vivid compounds - trace chromium makes rubies red, emeralds green, and alexandrite shift color.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000094.subject: ph
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000094.question: What is cesium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000094.answer_short: An alkali metal that behaves chemically like sodium, potassium and rubidium. Wallach says cesium and potassium pair up inside the cell, which is also why taking extra potassium makes you lose cesium faster.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000095.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000095.question: How was cesium discovered?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000095.answer_short: In 1860 the German chemists Bunsen and Kirchhoff identified cesium by its spectral 'fingerprint' -- the colors of light it emits when heated. Its lines were sky-blue, so they named it from the Latin caesius, 'sky blue.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000096.subject: ph
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000096.question: Can making the body alkaline treat cancer?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000096.answer_short: Wallach presents cesium chloride as “high-pH therapy” — cesium enters the cancer cell and makes its interior alkaline. He says it has been recommended for all cancers, including sarcomas, bronchiogenic carcinoma and colon cancer.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000097.subject: copper
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000097.question: What is copper, and where does its name come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000097.answer_short: A soft reddish metal - only 0.007% of Earth's crust. Its name is Latin 'cuprum' ('from Cyprus,' where Rome mined it), and it was one of humanity's first metals.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000106.subject: copper
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000106.question: What are normal copper levels in the blood?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000106.answer_short: Average plasma copper is about 87-153 (women) and 89-137 (men) micrograms per deciliter, and ~90% of it rides on a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000111.subject: copper
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000111.question: What raises blood copper, and what is copper overload?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000111.answer_short: Copper roughly doubles in pregnancy and on the pill, and rises with infection, liver disease and pellagra; overload shows as copper Kayser-Fleischer rings in the eye.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000112.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000112.question: What is dysprosium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000112.answer_short: A soft, silvery rare-earth metal -- the 9th most abundant of the rare earths -- discovered in 1886 and named from the Greek for 'hard to get at.' Its magnetic alloys help CDs work, and in the body it collects in bone.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000113.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000113.question: What is erbium used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000113.answer_short: A scarce rare-earth metal (found 1843), alloyed with vanadium to improve workability; its most memorable use is tinting glass and enamel pink -- the pink glass of sunglasses and costume jewelry. In the body it settles in bone.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000114.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000114.question: What is europium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000114.answer_short: One of the rarest rare earths, isolated in 1901 and named for Europe; it is the softest of them and so reactive it bursts into flame in air above 150C. It is mined from the ores monazite and bastnasite.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000116.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000116.question: What is fluorine?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000116.answer_short: The smallest, lightest and most reactive halogen ('salt former') - a pale-yellow gas so reactive it never occurs free, locked instead in minerals like fluorite.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000117.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000117.question: Who discovered fluorine, and what does its name mean?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000117.answer_short: Henri Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize for first isolating pure fluorine (1886), after 75 years of effort; the name is Latin 'fluere,' to flow.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000118.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000118.question: Is fluoride an essential nutrient?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000118.answer_short: Wallach says yes in trace amounts - before 1972 it was only 'considered' essential for tooth enamel, then Schwarz proved it essential for animals and humans.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000120.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000120.question: How much fluoride is in and around us?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000120.answer_short: An adult skeleton can bank up to 2.6 g of fluoride, and the average American takes in ~4.4 mg a day from food, water, toothpaste and supplements combined.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000122.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000122.question: How widespread is water fluoridation?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000122.answer_short: About 10,000 U.S. towns fluoridate water at 1 mg/L for 100 million people, reportedly cutting cavities 60-70% - but naturally high levels mottle children's teeth.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000124.subject: fluoride
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000124.question: Is fluoridated water safe?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000124.answer_short: Wallach calls it 'still highly controversial' - laying out both the cavity benefit and the fluorosis, bone-fracture and cancer concerns without a flat verdict.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000125.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000125.question: What is iron, and where does it come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000125.answer_short: Iron is the 4th most abundant element in Earth's crust — its ores opened the Iron Age (~1100 B.C.), and Earth's molten core is thought to be magnetized iron.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000127.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000127.question: Why is carbon monoxide so deadly?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000127.answer_short: Carbon monoxide binds the iron in hemoglobin ~200x more tightly than oxygen — crowding oxygen out of the blood, which is what makes it poisonous.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000128.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000128.question: How much iron is in your body, and where?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000128.answer_short: A healthy adult carries 3-5 g of iron; ~60-70% is 'functional' (in hemoglobin, muscle and enzymes) and 30-40% is stored in marrow and liver.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000130.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000130.question: What causes iron deficiency?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000130.answer_short: Wallach's list: unsupplemented pregnancy, heavy periods, chronic infection or bleeding, low stomach acid, diarrhea, and poor absorption from high-fiber diets.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000132.subject: iron
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000132.question: What helps or blocks iron absorption?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000132.answer_short: Stomach acid and vitamin C boost iron absorption; fiber and phytates block it — so Wallach says the 18 mg RDA is too low for vegans and high-fiber diets.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000134.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000134.question: What is gallium - the metal that melts in your hand?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000134.answer_short: A soft, aluminum-like metal so low-melting it liquefies from your body heat, yet has the widest liquid range of any metal; named for Gallia (the Latin name for France).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000136.subject: gallium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000136.question: Is gallium used in cancer medicine?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000136.answer_short: Yes - gallium-67 (78-hour half-life), one of medicine's first man-made isotopes, gathers in cancers like melanoma, letting it treat them without damage to surrounding tissues.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000137.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000137.question: Where is gadolinium found?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000137.answer_short: A rare-earth mineral scattered through rocks and plants -- hickory trees can concentrate it to 70 ppm -- and in land animals it collects in the bone and liver almost as soon as it is absorbed.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000138.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000138.question: What is germanium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000138.answer_short: A metalloid 'semiconductor' element predicted by Mendeleyev in 1871 and isolated in 1886 - 'doped' with a trace of arsenic or gallium, it makes transistors.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000141.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000141.question: How does germanium behave in the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000141.answer_short: It accepts and passes electrons like a semiconductor; biologically Wallach calls it an 'electrical impulse initiator' in cells and a cofactor for oxygen use.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000142.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000142.question: How was germanium's healing reputation discovered?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000142.answer_short: In 1950 the Japanese chemist Dr. Kazuhiko Asai found germanium in fossilized plants, and Russian researchers soon attributed anti-cancer activity to it.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000143.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000143.question: How does germanium support the immune system?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000143.answer_short: Asai tied germanium-rich herbs to healing; germanium boosts natural killer cells, interferon-gamma, macrophages and T-suppressor cells.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000144.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000144.question: What is Ge-132, the germanium supplement?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000144.answer_short: An organic, chelated germanium (carboxyethyl germanium sesquioxide) Asai made in 1967 - absorbed at ~30% and fully excreted within a week.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000146.subject: germanium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000146.question: Why are the 'Holy Waters' of Lourdes said to heal?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000146.answer_short: Wallach's mineral explanation: the famous healing waters of Lourdes, France contain large amounts of germanium and lithium.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000147.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000147.question: What is hydrogen?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000147.answer_short: The simplest atom -- one proton, one electron -- and the most abundant element in the universe (~93% of all atoms). As a gas it is diatomic (H2), colorless and highly flammable, burning with oxygen to make water; its name is Greek for 'water-maker.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000148.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000148.question: Who discovered hydrogen?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000148.answer_short: Henry Cavendish (1731-1810), who made the gas in 1766 - a brilliant, painfully shy recluse who never spoke to women and gave servants orders by written note.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000149.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000149.question: What does hydrogen have to do with the Hindenburg?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000149.answer_short: Hydrogen's lightness made it the early lift gas for blimps - until a spark ignited the hydrogen-filled Hindenburg in 1937 and the industry switched to helium.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000150.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000150.question: How does hydrogen set the body's acid-base balance?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000150.answer_short: Regulating acid-base balance is really regulating hydrogen-ion (H+) levels - healthy blood is held in a narrow pH band of 7.36-7.44 by homeostatic mechanisms.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000151.subject: ph
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000151.question: What is a normal blood pH?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000151.answer_short: Healthy blood runs 7.36 to 7.44. Below 7.30 is acidosis, above 7.44 is alkalosis, and below 6.8 or above 7.8 is rapidly fatal; inside cells pH runs 6.0 to 7.4.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000152.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000152.question: How does the body get rid of acid?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000152.answer_short: The kidneys excrete metabolic hydrogen ions ~60% as ammonium and 40% as weak acids; the trace of free H+ left is what sets the urine's pH.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000154.subject: hydrogen
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000154.question: Where is hydrogen found in the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000154.answer_short: Beyond water (70% of the body), hydrogen is a major part of nearly every biological molecule - carbohydrates, fats, proteins, enzymes, and DNA and RNA.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000155.subject: margarine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000155.question: Is margarine bad for you?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000155.answer_short: The hydrogenated and partially-hydrogenated vegetable oils sold as a safe substitute for butter — to prevent hardened arteries, fatty plaque and stroke — are now known to be a direct cause of those very diseases.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000156.subject: helium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000156.question: What is helium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000156.answer_short: The lightest noble gas -- so inert it forms no compounds and occurs pure in nature. After hydrogen it is the 2nd most abundant element in the universe (~7% of atoms). It was discovered on the sun before it was found on Earth -- seen in the sun's spectrum in 1868 and named from Greek Helios, 'sun.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000157.subject: helium
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000157.question: Why do deep-sea divers breathe helium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000157.answer_short: Because helium dissolves in blood far less than nitrogen, so less gas builds up under pressure and the risk of 'the bends' drops. The bends hits when a diver surfaces too fast and dissolved gas fizzes out of the blood into the joints -- like a just-opened soda.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000158.subject: obscure_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000158.question: Why was hafnium discovered so late?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000158.answer_short: Because it hid inside its chemical 'twin' zirconium -- common in the crust but nearly impossible to separate, so it was not isolated until 1923. Coster and de Hevesy named it Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor Niels Bohr's home city.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000159.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000159.question: What is mercury?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000159.answer_short: Mercury (Hg) is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature — a dense, silvery 'quicksilver' found in the bright-red ore cinnabar.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000160.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000160.question: How does mercury poison the body?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000160.answer_short: Mercury is an accumulative poison that binds to enzymes and cripples them; its vapor is far more dangerous than the liquid metal.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000161.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000161.question: What does mercury have to do with the quest for immortality?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000161.answer_short: Ancient Chinese alchemists drank mercury as an immortality elixir — China's first emperor poisoned himself to death that way.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000162.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000162.question: Where does mercury exposure come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000162.answer_short: Industry, mining, farming, vaccines and dental amalgam fillings concentrate mercury in the environment — even in people whose only exposure is their fillings.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000163.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000163.question: Is the mercury in fish dangerous?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000163.answer_short: Fish carry mercury as persistent methylmercury; heavy fish-eaters hold far more, and unlike inorganic mercury it crosses the placenta into the fetus.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000164.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000164.question: What protects against mercury poisoning?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000164.answer_short: Selenium is mercury's natural antidote: the two are mutually antagonistic, and selenium shields the kidneys and fetus from mercury.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000165.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000165.question: Can dental mercury fillings affect gut bacteria?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000165.answer_short: In monkeys, vapor from dental amalgam raised antibiotic-resistant gut bacteria from 9% to 70% — dropping back to 12% once the fillings were removed.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000166.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000166.question: Why do we say 'mad as a hatter'?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000166.answer_short: The phrase comes from real poisoning: Victorian hatmakers who brushed mercury paste onto felt inhaled the vapor and went 'mad as a hatter.'

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000167.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000167.question: Is dental mercury linked to MS, ALS or Parkinson's?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000167.answer_short: Wallach reports dentists and patients develop high rates of MS, ALS and Parkinson's tied to mercury vapor — he cites Annette Funicello's MS.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000168.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000168.question: What are the signs of mercury poisoning?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000168.answer_short: Mostly neurological: tremors, vertigo, irritability, mood changes, salivation, mouth inflammation and diarrhea — organic mercury is the most toxic.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000169.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000169.question: What was the Minamata disaster?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000169.answer_short: In 1962 a Japanese factory dumped mercury into Minamata Bay; contaminated fish caused an epidemic of birth defects, cerebral palsy and infant death.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000170.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000170.question: What happened in the Iraq mercury poisoning?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000170.answer_short: Iraqis ate bread from seed grain treated with mercury fungicide — thousands of babies were born with brain defects, cerebral palsy and neural-tube defects.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000171.subject: mercury
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000171.question: Do vaccines cause autism?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000171.answer_short: Wallach gives both sides — the mercury-preservative (thimerosal) hypothesis and his doubt that no other country saw the same autism surge — and leaves it open.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000172.subject: rare_earth_elements
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000172.question: What is holmium?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000172.answer_short: A rare-earth metal the body carries in trace amounts, mostly in bone. Spotted by its spectral 'fingerprint' in 1878 as unknown 'element X,' it was isolated in 1879 and named Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000173.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000173.question: Where is iodine found in nature?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000173.answer_short: Thinly spread through rock, water and soil — large areas of crust are iodine-free (it binds to humus), while seaweeds concentrate it up to 1,500 ppm.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000175.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000175.question: Where does commercial iodine come from?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000175.answer_short: Extracted from sodium iodate in Chilean saltpeter, from burnt-seaweed ash historically, and from underground brine wells in Arkansas and Oklahoma.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000176.subject: iodine
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000176.question: What is iodine used for?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000176.answer_short: A classic wound antiseptic (iodine tincture) and water purifier; in medicine, radioactive iodine-131 treats thyroid cancer and an overactive thyroid.
